summary: Defines procedures for specifying and registering media types for use in MIME and other Internet protocols. It is a Best Current Practice and was later replaced by RFC 6838.

plainLanguage.summary:
Protocols such as MIME can carry any kind of content, as long as the content carries a label that says what it is. This RFC sets out how new labels are proposed, reviewed and recorded.

It also sorts labels into groups depending on who owns them, from the open standards tree to a personal tree for experiments.

subtitle: The rules for naming, describing and registering media types such as text/plain with IANA.

tldr.problem: Protocols such as MIME can carry arbitrary labelled content, so the labels need an orderly, well-specified and public registration process.
tldr.mechanism: Media types are registered with IANA in trees, standards, vendor and personal, that have different requirements, using a common naming syntax, a fixed registration template and a review by a media types reviewer.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4288 replaced RFC 2048 and moved the registration process out of the MIME document set. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 6838.

facts.label: Maximum name length
facts.value: 127 characters for type, subtype and parameter names

facts.label: Standards tree prefix
facts.value: None; names in this tree are not faceted

today: RFC 4288 is a Best Current Practice document that has been obsoleted by RFC 6838, and it had earlier obsoleted RFC 2048. RFC 6838 is the text to read for media type registration today.

sections.title: Why Media Types Are Registered
sections.content:
Many Internet protocols, MIME among them, are built so that they can carry arbitrary labelled content. Something has to label that content, and there has to be a process for adding new labels, so that the set of labels grows in an orderly, well-specified and public way. RFC 4288 defines the specification and registration procedures for media types, and uses the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) as the central registry.

The document records how the process came about. Media type registration was first defined for asynchronous Internet mail, where there was a need to limit the number of media types so that mail could still be read when the capabilities of the remote mail system were unknown. As media types moved into settings where proliferation was no longer a hindrance, the original procedure proved too restrictive and had to be generalised. That was first done in RFC 2048, but the procedure was still part of the MIME document set. RFC 4288 moves it into a separate document so that it is clearly independent of MIME.

This revision also tries, for the first time, to build restrictions on where a media type may be used into the registration itself, in a systematic way.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols such as MIME can carry any kind of content, as long as the content carries a label that says what it is. This RFC sets out how new labels are proposed, reviewed and recorded.

sections.title: The Registration Trees
sections.content:
To keep the process efficient and flexible, the RFC divides registrations into trees, distinguished by faceted names of the form tree.subtree...subtype.

The standards tree is for types of general interest to the Internet community. A registration there MUST be approved by the IESG and MUST correspond to a formal publication by a recognised standards body; for the IETF itself, the proposal MUST be published as an RFC. Names in this tree are normally not faceted, so they carry no dot. The owner of a standards tree registration is assumed to be the standards body itself, and changing it needs the same level of processing as the original registration.

The vendor tree is for media types tied to commercially available products. Anyone who needs to interchange files for a product may place a registration there, but the registration formally belongs to the vendor or organisation that produces the software or file format, and changes are made at their request. Registrations carry the leading facet vnd., optionally followed by a producer name, as in vnd.bigcompany.funnypictures.

The personal or vanity tree covers types created experimentally or as part of products that are not distributed commercially. It is distinguished by the leading facet prs., and the owner is the person or entity making the registration.

The special x. tree allows subtype names beginning x. for the same purposes as names beginning x-: unregistered, experimental, and for use only with the active agreement of the parties exchanging them. Types in this tree MUST NOT be registered, and the RFC discourages the use of both forms now that vendor and personal registration is simple.

From time to time, and as the community requires, IANA may with the advice and consent of the IESG create new top-level trees, for example so that a scientific society can register media types for its field. The quality of review in such a tree is expected to match the standards tree, and the creation is announced through an RFC approved by the IESG.
sections.plainLanguage: Registrations are sorted into groups depending on who owns them and how much review they need. A type that is a general standard goes in the standards tree, a type tied to one company's product goes in the vendor tree with a vnd. prefix, and an experimental or personal type goes in the personal tree with a prs. prefix.

sections.title: What a Registration Must Satisfy
sections.content:
A media type MUST function as an actual media format. Things that are better thought of as a transfer encoding, a charset, or a collection of separate entities of another type cannot be registered, so base64, for example, cannot be registered as a media type. This applies in every tree.

Every registered media type must have a type name and a subtype name, and together they identify it uniquely. Both are case-insensitive. Type and subtype names beginning with X- are reserved for experimental use and MUST NOT be registered, which parallels the restriction on the x. tree. The names must fit this syntax:

type-name = reg-name
subtype-name = reg-name
reg-name = 1*127reg-name-chars
reg-name-chars = ALPHA / DIGIT / "!" / "#" / "$" / "&" / "." / "+" / "-" / "^" / "_"

Because of the rules in RFC 3023, a media subtype that does not represent XML entities MUST NOT be given a name ending in +xml, and the RFC cautions that +suffix constructs should be used with care because they may clash with future suffix definitions. Using different names for the same media type is discouraged.

Media types may use parameters, and the names, values and meanings of any parameters must be fully specified when a media type is registered in the standards tree, and should be as complete as possible in the other trees. There is no defined syntax for parameter values, so registrations must specify it themselves. Every registered media type must employ a single, canonical data format, whatever tree it is in, and standards tree types must have a precise and openly available format specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The label has to name a real file format. A transfer encoding or a character set cannot be registered as a media type, and the name has to fit a fixed syntax that allows up to 127 characters.

sections.title: Top-Level Types and Encoding Considerations
sections.content:
The choice of top-level type name must take into account the nature of the media type, and new subtypes must conform to the restrictions of the top-level type. The RFC describes each of the initial set. The text type is for material that is principally textual in form, where a charset parameter may name the character set; plain text is seen simply as a linear sequence of characters, possibly interrupted by line breaks or page breaks. The image type indicates content that is one or more separate images needing hardware to display, audio indicates audio data, and video indicates a time-varying picture, possibly with colour and coordinated sound. The application type is for discrete data that no other type fits, particularly data that an application program must process before a user can view it, such as file transfers, spreadsheets, presentations and scheduling data. The multipart and message types are composite: they encapsulate zero or more objects, each labelled with its own media type, and their subtypes must conform to RFC 2046. A new top-level type can only be defined by a standards-track RFC.

The registration also records an encoding considerations field, which says what sort of data the media type consists of. The permitted values are 7bit for CRLF-delimited 7bit US-ASCII text, 8bit for CRLF-delimited 8bit text, binary for an unrestricted sequence of octets, and framed for a series of frames or packets without internal framing indicators. A framed media type cannot simply be stored in a file or carried as a plain stream of octets, so it is unsuitable for many traditional protocols; RTP is given as a transport that uses a framed encoding. The RFC notes that Internet mail traditionally was limited to 7bit US-ASCII text, which is why this field is recorded at all.
sections.plainLanguage: A type is registered under a top-level name that says what kind of content it is, such as text, image or application. The registration also says whether the content is plain text, binary, or a series of frames that only makes sense with a particular transport.

sections.title: Security Requirements for a Registration
sections.content:
An analysis of security issues MUST be done for every type registered in the standards tree; a similar analysis for the vendor and personal trees is encouraged but not required. Whatever the analysis says, descriptions of security issues must be as accurate as possible, and a statement that there are no security issues associated with a type MUST NOT be confused with a statement that the security issues have not been assessed. There is no requirement that media types be secure or free from risks, but all known security risks MUST be identified in the registration, in any tree.

The RFC lists the issues a security analysis should look at. Complex media types may include directives that institute actions on a recipient's files or other resources, and in many cases the originator is allowed to specify arbitrary actions with devastating effects; the registration of application/postscript in RFC 2046 is the example given. All registrations MUST state whether they use such active content, and if they do, what steps have been taken to protect users from harm. Complex media types may also carry directives that lead to disclosure of information that enables a later attack or violates a recipient's privacy. A media type that employs compression can be used to send a small amount of data that expands enormously on the receiver and consumes all of its resources, so registrations should state whether they compress and what steps guard against that. Finally, a media type might be aimed at applications that need a security assurance it does not itself provide, for example confidential medical information that relies on an external confidentiality service or is meant only for a secure environment.

The Security Considerations section of the RFC itself points back to these requirements and adds nothing further.
sections.plainLanguage: Every registration has to say what could go wrong if a recipient opens the content, and it must not claim there is no risk unless that has actually been checked.

sections.title: The Registration Procedure
sections.content:
The registration procedure is not a formal standards process but an administrative one, meant to allow community comment and sanity checking without much delay. For a standards tree registration by the IETF, the normal IETF processes apply: an Internet Draft is posted first, and then a notice of the registration MUST be sent to the ietf-types@iana.org mailing list for review. The intent of that posting is to get comments on the choice of name, on whether the references are unambiguous, and on the interoperability and security considerations. The submitter may post a revised registration or abandon it at any time. Vendor and personal tree registrations go straight to IANA, ideally after a first posting to the same list.

Standards tree registrations MUST be approved by the IESG before registration, and the IANA will only register a standards tree type in response to a communication from the IESG saying it is approved. Where the registration is part of an RFC publication request or a standards tree submission, that approval in effect submits it to IANA and no separate request is needed. Registrations sent to IANA are passed to the media types reviewer, appointed by the IETF Applications Area Directors, who checks the registration against the requirements in this document; anything that does not meet them goes back to the submitter, and the reviewer's decisions may be appealed to the IESG.

Once a type is registered, the owner may request a change, and the same procedure as for the original request is used. Changes should be requested only for serious omissions or errors, and a change may be denied if it would render entities that were valid under the old definition invalid under the new one. Ownership can be transferred by telling IANA and the ietf-types list, and the IESG may reassign responsibility, most often when the original author can no longer make changes. Registrations may not be deleted: a type that is no longer believed appropriate can be declared OBSOLETE through a change to its intended use field.
sections.plainLanguage: A new type is proposed, posted to a mailing list for comment, approved by the IESG if it belongs in the standards tree, and then recorded by IANA after a reviewer checks it against these rules. The owner can ask for changes later, but a registration is never deleted.

children.note: Approved by the IESG and tied to a formal publication.

children.label: Special x. tree
